title: (Extra) The Wolf You Feed: pay attention!
author: Julian Girdham
summary: Written up from his researchED Cork talk, Julian Girdham's essay argues that attention is both the foundation of learning and an ethical question for teachers. He gathers voices from Willingham, Callard, Pollan, Maryanne Wolf and L.M. Sacasas to show that attention is a limited capacity and that the online "uni-context" now forces students into a draining top-down struggle to manage it. He sets out the classroom factors that fragment attention and cites teacher surveys and the 2025 PISA report on declining sustained reading, while insisting, with Nilli Lavie and Julia Bell, that the underlying capacity remains and can be trained. As a secondary English teacher, he makes the case for demanding texts, close reading and the guiding question of whether a task will help students think. The essay ends by warning that AI is an environment rather than a neutral tool, framed by the parable of the two wolves.
points: Girdham treats attention as an ethical issue in education, since many contemporary crises are failures of attention to what it is to be human.
Agnes Callard's distinction between bottom-up and top-down attention explains why students and adults now feel at war with themselves.
Andrew Cantarutti's image of walled-garden schools frames classrooms as deliberately protected spaces for deep attention.
PISA 2025 data showing more hasty readers and steeper late-test declines point to a falling capacity for careful reading and sustained attention.
Demanding poetry such as Derek Mahon's Antarctica is defended as the right kind of challenge, because intense attention is what real thinking requires.
quotes: I agree. It is increasingly clear to me that in education the question of attention is also an ethical issue. So many of the most extreme and disturbing features of our contemporary world (climate change, war and genocide in parts of the world, the disturbances of social media, the possibility of AI being an existential threat) are failures of attention to what it is to be human.
Almost all teachers feel that attention is declining. A Cambridge International Survey in 2025 found that 88% of teachers believed their students’ attention spans are becoming shorter.

Attention is a limited capacity system, and always proceeds to capacity: it is not possible to look up to see who has opened the door, and at the same time keep back 40% of your attention for continuing to write notes on the current topic.

People can still sustain attention, and it would be absurd to suggest that in the tiny number of years since online technology developed, evolution has had any effect on the human brain. The real ability to attend is still there.

And so it should: we are doing a disservice to our students if we decide that they cannot handle demanding material. Even more dismaying is the tendency of educational authorities to reduce the quality and depth of curricular material
The key to everything I do in class nowadays is a single question always hovering at the back of my brain: will this help them to think?
Thinking, and close reading, and attention to story, are three principles of what I am doing in the classroom, and they are all linked to the idea of attention.

The book was published in 2018 before the public launch of ChatGPT, but that last question is now heightened in the age of publicly available AI. I love that phrase ‘storehouses of knowledge’, but the tedious old misconception ‘they can just Google it now’ has been turbo-charged by AI.
